title: Cardiovascular Changes in Women May Start 20 Years Before Menopause
text:
Cardiovascular Changes in Women May Start 20 Years Before Menopause
A new study indicates that cardiovascular changes in women may initiate as much as two decades before menopause, contesting the commonly held belief that these changes are primarily triggered by hormonal fluctuations during midlife. Published in the journal Hypertension on September 14, the research suggests that pulse pressure—which reflects the difference between the systolic and diastolic numbers in a blood pressure reading—begins to rise in women in their late 30s, approximately ten years earlier than in men.
Research conducted by tracking data from over 6,500 women and more than 3,000 men involved in the Framingham Heart Study, one of the longest ongoing cardiovascular research projects, assessed participants over three health evaluations spanning a period of 14 years. The analysis revealed that women's pulse pressure reached its lowest point and then began to significantly rise earlier than that of their male counterparts. Specifically, the shift in women was noted around their late 30s, while men experienced this change in their late 40s.
Notably, these findings remained consistent irrespective of the timing of menopause for women. By the time women reached 60, their pulse pressure was consistently higher than that of men.
Gary F. Mitchell, one of the study's investigators, commented, "To our huge surprise, our results suggest that factors other than the timing of the final menstrual period were likely involved in the accelerated increase in pulse pressure in women after midlife."
Pulse pressure is linked to the aorta, the largest blood vessel in the body, which carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the circulatory system. As age progresses, the walls of the aorta tend to become stiffer and less elastic. Consequently, the heart faces increased exertion to pump blood throughout the body.
The widening of pulse pressure is increasingly recognised as a critical indicator of cardiovascular health. High pulse pressure has associations with elevated risks of heart disease, dementia, and kidney issues. Furthermore, it may complicate high blood pressure management, as certain medications can prove less effective when arteries exhibit stiffness.
The study underscores the importance of early monitoring and attention to women’s cardiovascular health well before midlife. Researchers advocate for regular assessments of pulse pressure, as this may enable healthcare providers to identify potential heart-related risks earlier in women's lives.
